title: Headless Commerce Business Case Builder for APAC Teams
summary: A headless commerce business case builder for APAC e-commerce directors: real pricing, three-year TCO modelling, a weighted scoring matrix and risk mitigations.
body_markdown:
**Quick Answer:** A headless commerce business case for APAC needs four things: weighted evaluation criteria set before platform selection, a three-year TCO including 15–25% annual front-end maintenance, revenue modelled in three scenarios with a stated break-even uplift, and phased delivery with measurable stop gates.


---


Success looks like this: eighteen months after go-live, your mobile conversion rate is up, your marketing team ships a landing page in a day instead of a sprint, and your CFO can point at the P&L and see where the migration money went. Nobody is still talking about the replatform. That is the only outcome worth writing a business case for.


*Related reading:*[Shopify Plus APAC Merchant Case Studies: The Monitoring Gap](https://branch8.com/posts/shopify-plus-apac-merchant-case-studies-error-monitoring-benchmarks)


*Related reading:*[Adobe Commerce to Shopify Plus Migration Playbook: 9 Phased Steps](https://branch8.com/posts/adobe-commerce-to-shopify-plus-migration-playbook)


Most headless proposals die long before that, and not because the architecture is wrong. They die because the e-commerce director walked into a capital committee with a slide about APIs and composable architecture, and walked out with a request to "come back with numbers." This headless commerce business case builder for APAC teams is the structure I would use to get those numbers — total cost of ownership modelled honestly, performance uplift benchmarked against published data rather than vendor decks, and a risk register that pre-empts the questions your CFO will ask in minute four.


*Related reading:*[Shopify Plus vs Adobe Commerce: 2026 Comparison for APAC](https://branch8.com/posts/shopify-plus-vs-adobe-commerce-2026-comparison-apac)


*Related reading:*[PostgreSQL Database Performance Benchmarking for APAC Retail Data](https://branch8.com/posts/postgresql-database-performance-benchmarking-apac-retail)


*Related reading:*[Staff Augmentation vs Managed Squad: APAC Tech Decision Guide](https://branch8.com/posts/staff-augmentation-vs-managed-squad-apac-tech)


I'll be direct about the trade-offs. Headless is more expensive to run than a monolith for most mid-market retailers. If your business case does not acknowledge that, your finance team will find it anyway, and you lose credibility on everything else in the deck.


## Start With Evaluation Criteria, Not Platform Shortlists


The single most common mistake I see in APAC replatform proposals: the deck opens with a vendor comparison. That signals you picked an answer and reverse-engineered a justification.


Build your criteria first, weight them, and only then let platforms compete. Here is the criteria set that survives executive scrutiny.


### Commercial criteria


- **Three-year TCO delta** versus staying on your current stack, including the do-nothing cost of deferred maintenance.
- **Revenue mechanism** — be specific about whether uplift comes from conversion rate, average order value, new channel revenue, or market expansion. "Better experience" is not a mechanism.
- **Margin of safety** — what conversion uplift do you need just to break even? If the answer is above 15%, the case is fragile.
- **Cash flow shape** — headless front-loads cost. A committee that funds annually may prefer a phased migration even if total cost is higher.


### Operational criteria


- **Content velocity** — how many days from brief to published campaign page today, and what is the target?
- **Team capability** — do you have, or can you hire, front-end engineers comfortable with React/Vue and a Jamstack build pipeline? In Hong Kong, Singapore and Sydney that talent is expensive and contested. In Taipei, Ho Chi Minh City and Kuala Lumpur the economics differ substantially.
- **Dependency count** — each additional SaaS component in a composable stack is another vendor contract, another SLA, another renewal negotiation.


### Technical criteria


- **Channel requirement** — do you genuinely need to serve the same catalogue to web, native app, in-store POS, kiosk, marketplace and a WeChat Mini Program? Multi-channel is the strongest headless argument in APAC and the weakest one in single-channel businesses.
- **Integration surface** — ERP, WMS, loyalty, local payment rails. In APAC this is not trivial: Alipay, WeChat Pay, FPS in Hong Kong, PayNow in Singapore, PromptPay in Thailand, GrabPay across Southeast Asia.
- **Performance ceiling** — what is your current Largest Contentful Paint on 4G, and what is physically achievable on your existing template architecture?


### Regulatory and regional criteria


- **Data residency** — Hong Kong's PDPO, Singapore's PDPA, Australia's Privacy Act, and China's PIPL all impose different obligations. A decoupled architecture can actually help here, because you can localise the data layer without rebuilding the storefront.
- **Localisation depth** — Traditional Chinese, Simplified Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Thai and Bahasa all have typographic and input requirements that a decoupled front end handles more cleanly than a theme-override approach.


## The Performance Numbers That Actually Move a Committee


Your CFO does not care about Lighthouse scores. They care about the chain from milliseconds to money. Build that chain explicitly with third-party data, not vendor claims.


Google's research with Deloitte, published as *Milliseconds Make Millions* , found that a 0.1 second improvement in mobile site speed increased retail conversion rates by 8.4% and average order value by 9.2%. That is the most useful single statistic in any headless business case because it is from a credible source and expresses the link in commercial terms.


Supporting evidence worth including:


- **Google/SOASTA** research found that as page load time goes from one second to three seconds, the probability of bounce increases 32%, and to five seconds, 90%.
- **Google's Core Web Vitals thresholds** — LCP under 2.5 seconds, INP under 200 milliseconds, CLS under 0.1 — give you an objective pass/fail target rather than a subjective "faster." Pull your current field data from the Chrome UX Report before you write a word of the proposal.
- **Akamai's** long-cited retail research put the cost of a 100-millisecond delay at roughly 7% in conversions. Older, but still quoted in board papers.


The honest framing: these are correlational benchmarks across large samples, not guarantees for your catalogue. Use them to model a range, not a point estimate. I model three scenarios — a conservative 3% conversion uplift, a base case of 7%, and an upside of 12% — and I show the committee the break-even line on all three.


One more thing on performance. If your current site is slow because of a bloated theme, forty marketing tags and unoptimised hero images, headless will not fix that. You can recover a large share of the available performance gain by fixing those on your existing platform for a fraction of the cost. Say this in your deck before someone else does. It makes every other claim more believable.

## Pricing: What Headless Actually Costs in APAC


Here are real published list figures and realistic implementation ranges. Verify current pricing directly with vendors — these change.


### Platform licensing (annual)


- **Shopify Plus** — from USD 2,300 per month on a three-year term, or USD 2,500 month-to-month, per Shopify's published pricing, with variable platform fees above certain GMV thresholds. Hydrogen and Oxygen (Shopify's React framework and hosting) are included, which makes Plus the cheapest credible entry point into headless for most mid-market APAC retailers.
- **BigCommerce Enterprise** — quote-based, commonly landing in the USD 15,000–60,000 per year band depending on order volume and API call tiers.
- **commercetools** — quote-based enterprise contracts, typically starting in the low-to-mid six figures USD annually for enterprise tiers. Strong fit for multi-brand, multi-country catalogues; overkill for a single-market retailer.
- **Salesforce Commerce Cloud** — priced primarily on a percentage of gross merchandise value, historically in the 1–3% range depending on volume and tier. At scale this becomes the dominant line item in your TCO.
- **Open-source options** — Medusa, Saleor and Vendure have no licence fee. Your cost moves entirely into engineering and hosting, which can be the right trade in markets where developer cost is lower, but it transfers platform risk onto your team.


### Supporting SaaS components


- **Contentful** — Premium tiers are quote-based; the published Lite tier starts around USD 300 per month. Enterprise content platforms commonly run USD 25,000–100,000+ per year.
- **Sanity, Storyblok, Strapi Cloud** — meaningfully cheaper, often USD 5,000–30,000 annually at mid-market scale.
- **Search (Algolia, Constructor)** — usage-priced; budget USD 10,000–50,000 per year at mid-market volumes.
- **Hosting and edge (Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare)** — Vercel Enterprise typically begins around USD 25,000 per year; self-managed edge hosting on Cloudflare can be an order of magnitude cheaper with more engineering overhead.


### Implementation


For an APAC mid-market retailer with one to three markets, a standard catalogue and two or three back-office integrations, a headless storefront build realistically lands in the USD 80,000–250,000 range. Multi-country, multi-currency, multi-language with ERP and POS integration pushes that to USD 250,000–600,000+. Enterprise composable programmes at commercetools or Salesforce scale routinely exceed USD 1 million across a multi-year roadmap.


Regional delivery economics matter and should be in your deck. Blended senior full-stack rates differ materially across Hong Kong, Singapore, Sydney, Taipei, Kuala Lumpur and Ho Chi Minh City. A managed-contracting model that places the architect in your timezone and the build team in a lower-cost APAC market is how many global brands fund an APAC headless programme they could not justify at London or San Francisco rates. The trade-off is coordination overhead — you need genuine technical leadership on your side, or you pay for rework.


### The line item everyone forgets


Ongoing front-end maintenance. A decoupled storefront is software you now own. Budget 15–25% of the initial build cost annually for framework upgrades, dependency patching, API version migrations and browser compatibility. On a monolith, your platform vendor absorbs most of this. On headless, you do. This is the single biggest reason headless TCO exceeds monolith TCO at mid-market scale, and leaving it out of the model is how business cases get retroactively destroyed in year two.


## A Scoring Framework You Can Run in an Afternoon


Score each dimension 1–5, multiply by the weight, and sum. The framework exists to make disagreement explicit — when two executives score "channel complexity" as 2 and 5, that is the conversation worth having, not the total.


### Dimension 1 — Channel complexity (weight 25%)


- 1: Single web storefront, one market.
- 3: Web plus app, or web plus marketplace feeds.
- 5: Web, native app, POS, kiosk, marketplaces and social commerce across three or more APAC markets with a shared catalogue.


### Dimension 2 — Content and campaign velocity need (weight 20%)


- 1: Fewer than one campaign page per month; merchandising rarely changes.
- 3: Weekly campaign cadence, seasonal peaks.
- 5: Daily merchandising changes, multi-market campaign calendars, flash-sale mechanics typical of Singles' Day and 11.11 cycles.


### Dimension 3 — Current performance gap (weight 20%)


- 1: Already passing Core Web Vitals on mobile field data.
- 3: LCP between 2.5 and 4 seconds; recoverable with optimisation.
- 5: LCP above 4 seconds, structurally constrained by the current template or platform.


### Dimension 4 — Engineering capability (weight 15%)


- 1: No in-house front-end engineering; agency-dependent with no technical owner.
- 3: One or two engineers plus a reliable delivery partner.
- 5: Standing front-end team with CI/CD maturity and on-call ownership.


### Dimension 5 — Integration and localisation complexity (weight 10%)


- 1: Stock payment methods, no ERP integration.
- 5: Multiple regional payment rails, ERP/WMS sync, loyalty, and three or more languages.


### Dimension 6 — Financial headroom (weight 10%)


- 1: No capital available; cost-out mandate in force.
- 5: Funded multi-year digital programme with committed opex increase.


**Reading the score.** Below 2.5 weighted average: stay on your current platform and spend the money on performance optimisation and conversion work. Between 2.5 and 3.5: consider a hybrid — Shopify Plus with a Hydrogen storefront for key pages, or a headless CMS layered onto an existing checkout. Above 3.5: a full headless business case is defensible, and the scoring sheet itself becomes an appendix in your proposal.

## Structuring the Proposal Document Itself


The business case is a document with a job: get a decision. Nine sections, in this order.


1. **The commercial problem in one paragraph.** Not the architecture. Something like: mobile accounts for the majority of sessions but a minority of revenue, and the gap has widened for six consecutive quarters.
2. **Current-state baseline.** Core Web Vitals field data, conversion by device, campaign lead time in days, and the engineering hours consumed by platform workarounds last year. Numbers only.
3. **Options considered — including do nothing.** Always include optimise-in-place as a genuine option, costed. Committees trust proposals that argue against themselves.
4. **Recommended architecture.** One diagram. Name the components and the reason each exists.
5. **Three-year TCO.** Licence, implementation, maintenance, hosting, internal headcount, and the do-nothing comparison. Show the year-two maintenance line prominently.
6. **Revenue model with three scenarios.** Conservative, base, upside. State the break-even uplift required.
7. **Risk register with mitigations.** Covered below.
8. **Phasing and decision gates.** Each phase ends with a measurable gate and an explicit option to stop.
9. **What we will measure and when.** Pre-commit to the metrics so nobody redefines success later.


### The APAC-specific sections to add


If you operate across more than one APAC market, add a market sequencing section. Which market goes first, and why? Usually it is the one with the highest mobile traffic share and the simplest payment and tax configuration — not the largest revenue market, because you do not want your highest-revenue market to be the learning exercise.


Also add a data residency note. Under PIPL, cross-border transfer of personal information out of mainland China carries specific obligations; Singapore's PDPA and Hong Kong's PDPO take different approaches to transfer and consent. A decoupled data layer gives you more options, and saying so turns a compliance headache into a supporting argument.


## Risk Mitigation Arguments That Pre-Empt the Hard Questions


Four risks will be raised. Answer them in the document before they are asked out loud.


### "What if the migration tanks our SEO?"


This is the legitimate one. Replatforms damage organic traffic when URL structures change without mapping, when rendering strategy regresses, or when structured data is dropped. Mitigations to name explicitly: a complete 301 map validated pre-launch, server-side rendering or static generation rather than client-side-only rendering for indexable pages, preserved canonical and hreflang tags across language variants, and a crawl comparison using Screaming Frog or Sitebulb before and after. Commit to a two-week traffic hold-back gate before decommissioning the old stack.


### "What if we cannot hire the team?"


Honest answer: in Hong Kong, Singapore and Australia, senior front-end engineers with commerce experience are genuinely scarce. Mitigation is structural — a managed-contracting arrangement that guarantees continuity of named engineers, with documented handover artefacts and a knowledge-transfer gate in each phase. Do not propose a model that depends on hiring three people you have not yet found.


### "What if the vendor changes pricing?"


Real risk, particularly with GMV-based pricing where your costs scale with your success. Mitigations: multi-year price locks where available, an abstraction layer between your storefront and the commerce API so the backend is replaceable, and a contractual cap on tier escalation.


### "What if it just costs more and does nothing?"


The strongest mitigation is phasing with real stop gates. Phase one: one high-traffic page template — category or product detail — rebuilt headless, running alongside the existing site with traffic split. Measure. If Core Web Vitals improve and conversion does not degrade, proceed. If not, you have spent a contained amount and learned something true. I have run this pattern with a listed Greater China jewellery retailer and with a manufacturer selling through a dealer network; in both cases the first phase changed the scope of the second, which is the entire point of building the gate.

## Common Objections and How to Answer Them


**"Shopify already does headless — why pay for commercetools?"** Often correct. Shopify Plus with Hydrogen and Oxygen covers a large share of mid-market APAC requirements at a fraction of enterprise composable cost. Reserve commercetools, Salesforce Commerce Cloud or Elastic Path for genuine multi-brand, multi-entity complexity.


**"Can't we use open-source and save the licence fee?"** Medusa, Saleor and Vendure remove licence cost and add engineering cost plus platform risk. Viable if you have a standing engineering team and a long time horizon. Not viable if your plan is one contractor and hope.


**"Isn't this just a CMS project?"** Sometimes yes, and that is good news. If your pain is campaign velocity rather than commerce logic, a headless CMS in front of your existing checkout delivers much of the value at a fraction of the cost and risk.


## How to Evaluate: Your Pre-Submission Checklist


Run this before your business case goes to committee. Every item should be a yes.


- \[ \] Core Web Vitals field data for your current site is in the document, pulled from CrUX or your real-user monitoring — not lab scores.
- \[ \] Do-nothing and optimise-in-place are both costed as genuine options.
- \[ \] Three-year TCO includes annual front-end maintenance at 15–25% of build cost.
- \[ \] Revenue uplift is modelled in three scenarios with a stated break-even threshold.
- \[ \] Every performance statistic cites a named external source.
- \[ \] Each phase has a measurable stop gate, not just a milestone.
- \[ \] SEO migration plan names the specific tooling and the hold-back period.
- \[ \] Team capability is addressed with a continuity mechanism, not a hiring assumption.
- \[ \] APAC market sequencing is justified, with first market chosen for learnability.
- \[ \] Data residency obligations across your operating markets are listed with the architectural response.
- \[ \] The scoring sheet is attached as an appendix with named scorers.
- \[ \] Success metrics and review dates are pre-committed in writing.


If more than two items are missing, you are not ready to submit. A headless commerce business case builder for APAC only works when the uncomfortable numbers are in it — the maintenance line, the break-even uplift, the honest admission that optimisation might get you most of the way for a tenth of the cost. Committees fund proposals from people who already found the holes.
